summary.text: 鸡 is the simplified Chinese form used for the word “chicken.” Its traditional graph 雞 is interpreted as having an early pictorial form and later forms analyzed with a bird element and sound-bearing 奚. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, which does not establish the picture’s original referent or the sequence of graphic development.

formation.text: The historical compound 雞 is phonosemantic: 隹 or 鳥 contributes the bird category, and 奚 supplies a sound cue. An earlier pictorial interpretation is reported, but the place-name use and incomplete dating do not establish a fully ordered transition from picture to compound. The visible shape 鸡 is not evidence for a historical 又 + 鸟 construction.

components.text: Early forms of 雞 are interpreted as a whole picture of a chicken, with the head, crest, and open beak emphasized. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent remains uncertain.

In 雞, 奚 serves as a sound element, not for its separate lexical meaning. Its modern Mandarin reading differs from 雞; the supplied Middle Chinese forms share a rhyme but differ in initial. The Old Chinese comparison is approximate.

sound_limitation.text: The Old Chinese comparison comes from a local data cross-check not verified at the dataset publisher; exact reconstructed readings are not independently established by the inspected sources. 奚’s phonetic role is explicitly stated in the historical dictionary account.

sound.text: The supplied Middle Chinese forms share a rhyme but differ in initial; modern Mandarin xī and jī also differ. The Old Chinese comparison is approximate, not an exact match.

components.text: 隹 is the bird-category element in Qin and later forms of 雞. Some Warring States Qi and Chu forms instead use 鳥, and the historical dictionary account calls 鷄 a Zhou-script form written with 鳥; the evidence does not establish one linear sequence between them.

鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and is listed as 鳮（雞） in the 1956 simplification scheme. The precise route from that form to entry character 鸡 is not established; 又 has no supported historical role here.

history.text: The selected oracle-script image is a modern redraw of a form interpreted as a chicken picture, not an ancient inscription. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. One account describes 奚 as later added as a sound marker when the picture could be confused with other birds, but a fully dated sequence is not established.

The bird element varies across the record: some Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin and later forms use 隹. 鷄 is described as a Zhou-script form with 鳥 and is treated as a graphic variant of 雞; a single linear path between these forms is not established.
The 1956 simplification scheme lists 鳮（雞） and simplifies 鳥 as 鸟. It does not document the precise graphic route to 鸡 or support analyzing 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound.

uncertainties.text: Early 雞 is interpreted as a chicken picture, but the earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. The picture’s original referent, earliest lexical meaning, and chronology of any transition to a compound remain uncertain.
The bird element appears as both 鳥 and 隹 in different script traditions and periods. The evidence does not establish a complete sequence or show that 鳥 was only a later replacement.
The simplification evidence associates 鳮 with 雞 and lists 鳮（雞）, but does not document the precise graphic steps to standardized 鸡.

senses.text: A Qin bamboo-slip passage is reported using 雞 for chicken. The oracle-bone place-name use does not show whether this was the graph’s earliest animal meaning.

senses.period: oracle-bone script tradition; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: An oracle-bone use of 雞 is reported as a place name. This attests a graph use but does not establish the name’s referent or the graph’s original lexical meaning.

senses.gloss: 谿, valley or stream, written with 雞
senses.period: Mawangdui manuscript witness; exact borrowing date unresolved
senses.text: In a Mawangdui text, 雞 is reported as a phonetic loan for 谿, “valley” or “stream”; another manuscript copy has 溪. The sign 雞 was reused to write a different word rather than “chicken” developing into “valley.” The report gives no contemporary pronunciations to demonstrate the proposed sound match.
The common current meaning is chicken.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone place-name use and Qin-slip animal use do not establish a direct semantic transition between them or identify the picture’s earliest lexical value.
The reported Mawangdui loan lacks contemporary pronunciations and a demonstrated sound rationale; its motivation and timing remain unresolved.

overview.text: 鸡 means “chicken.” The traditional graph 雞 is interpreted as an early chicken picture, with later forms analyzed as a compound containing a bird element and sound-bearing 奚. Its earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so that interpretation does not settle the graph’s original referent.

components.text: Early forms of 雞 are interpreted as a whole chicken picture, though the earliest reported use is a place name and the original referent is uncertain.
奚 supplies sound in 雞, not its separate meaning. The Middle Chinese comparison shares a rhyme but differs in initial; the Old Chinese match is approximate.
隹 supplies the bird category in Qin and later forms. Other traditions use 鳥, so the written bird element varies.
鳮 is associated with 雞 and listed as 鳮（雞） in the simplification scheme; the precise route from it to 鸡 is not documented.

takeaway.text: The evidence does not establish 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound; the visible shape alone cannot show that origin.

relationships.text: In the historical compound 雞, 奚 is explicitly identified as the sound-bearing element; this role belongs to 雞, not to simplified 鸡.
隹 contributes the bird category in Qin and later forms of 雞; other traditions and periods also write the bird element as 鳥.
鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and appears as 鳮（雞） in the simplification scheme; its precise route to standardized 鸡 is not established.
The 1956 scheme associates 鸡 with 鳮（雞） and simplifies 鳥 as 鸟; it does not support analyzing 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound.
